chapters.title: Read the chip city
chapters.text: Start overhead: a compute die sits beside HBM memory stacks, all supported by a silicon interposer. This teaching scene enlarges a tiny package into a city. First identify who computes, who stores data and who connects them; then descend into the details.

chapters.title: Three different levels
chapters.text: Lower the camera and separate the dies, interposer and package substrate. The interposer handles dense die-to-die routing; the substrate connects the assembly to the circuit board. This tour represents silicon-interposer 2.5D packaging, not every CoWoS variant, which can use different interconnect structures.

chapters.title: Short, wide data routes
chapters.text: Fly along the die edges and follow parallel connections toward HBM. Bandwidth comes from many channels working together, not simply from accelerating one wire. Glowing routes show connectivity rather than electron speed. Real design also evaluates parasitics, crosstalk and timing margin.

chapters.title: Separate assembly risks
chapters.text: Separate the dies, interposer and substrate before assembly. Inspect components, then plan placement, underfill and post-bond tests so defects are not discovered only after costly integration. This is a conceptual workflow: actual sequencing, materials and process conditions depend on the qualified manufacturing flow.

chapters.title: Connections between layers
chapters.text: In the separated layers, identify die contacts, interposer wiring and through-silicon vias. Vertical connections inside an HBM stack are not the same structures as connections through the interposer toward the substrate. Trace the distinct routes: data travels to neighboring dies, while power and external connections reach the substrate.

chapters.title: Bandwidth and energy together
chapters.text: Follow data from memory to compute and back. Ask three questions: how much data per second, how much energy per bit and what worst-case latency? Shorter links can help, but proximity alone does not guarantee lower system power. Workload, controllers and utilization also shape the result.

chapters.title: Heat has a route too
chapters.text: Heat leaves the compute die through interface material and cooling structures above it. Nearby memory also has temperature limits. The red region is an illustrative hotspot, not measured temperature. A fair cooling comparison holds power, ambient conditions and contact conditions constant.

chapters.title: Verify hidden connections
chapters.text: At inspection, visual checks, joint imaging and electrical tests answer different questions. A clean X-ray image does not prove every signal works; an electrical pass does not prove lifetime reliability. Connect defect locations, test results and process lots to identify meaningful corrective actions.

chapters.title: Bigger is not the only answer
chapters.text: Rise above the package and compare more memory, shorter routes and manufacturability. Package area, warpage, power delivery and cooling interact with cost and yield. The interposer is valuable because it enables a balanced system, not because every available location is filled with silicon.

chapters.title: Take away a complete route
chapters.text: Finish with the complete route: define requirements, place compute and HBM, design interconnect and power, plan assembly, then verify thermal behavior and reliability. If you can show where data begins, where heat leaves and which connection needs evidence, you understand the core of this package.
